Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.42 7.2 The signature function Definition 7.2.1. (Signature function.) Consider g ∈ Sn and the variables x1, x2, . . . , xn. We can think of g as a permutation of the variables, with gxk = xgk. (E.g. If g = (1 2 3) ∈ S3 then gx1 = x2, gx2 = x3, gx3 = x1.) We now define a special polynomial: ∆ = ∏ i<j (xi − xj) = ((x1 − x2)⋯(x1 − xn))((x2 − x3)⋯(x2 − xn))⋯((xn−1 − xn)) (E.g. In S3 we have ∆ = (x1 − x2)(x1 − x3)(x2 − x3).) What do permutations in Sn do to ∆? (E.g. In S3: • e sends ∆ → ∆ • (1 2) sends ∆ → (x2 − x1)(x2 − x3)(x1 − x3) = −∆ • (1 3) sends ∆ → (x3 − x2)(x3 − x1)(x2 − x1) = −∆ In general case: every permutation in Sn sends ∆ to ±∆. We define a map σ ∶ Sn → {1, −1} called the signature function on Sn as follows: σ(g) = { 1 if g maps ∆ to ∆ −1 if g maps ∆ to −∆. If σ(g) = 1 we say g is even, and if σ(g) = −1 we say g is odd. What is the point?!. The signature function divides Sn into two sets (even and odd). We can use this to define a new group that is one of the most important groups there is. Proposition 7.2.2. Recall that {1, −1} is a group under multiplication. The function σ ∶ Sn → {1, −1} is a homomorphism. Proof. This is an easy proof. Fix g, h ∈ Sn. Then (because σ(g) is just ±1) we have: (gh)∆ = g(h∆) = g(σ(h)∆) = σ(h)(g∆) = σ(h)σ(g)∆ = σ(g)σ(h)∆. Hence σ(gh) = σ(g)σ(h). Note: all the above is the definition of σ, but it’s a horrible way to calculate σ. In fact there is an easy way, but we will have to prove some results first. Corollary 7.2.3. (Very important!) Let g ∈ Sn; we know already we can write g as a product of cycles, g = c1c2 . . . cm. Suppose cycle ci has length ri for i = 1, . . . , m. Then σ(ci) = (−1) ri−1, and therefore, σ(g) = σ(c1)σ(c2)⋯σ(cm) = (−1) (r1−1)⋯(−1)(rm−1). Example 7.2.4. The signature of g = (15742)(129) is σ(g) = (−1)5−1(−1) 3−1 = 1, so g is even. Proposition 7.2.5. If g ∈ Sn is a permutation, then σ(g−1) = σ(g). Proof. Exercise. [Hint: first think about cycles, see handout for proof]. Remark 7.2.6. Notice that the signature of a function depends only on its cycle shape. Two permutations with the same cycle shape have the same signature!

Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.43 7.2.1 Handout for Section 7.2 Example 7.2.7. Here are some examples. 1. g = (1 7 3 4 2)(9 5 6)(8 11) ∈ S12 is odd because σ(g) = (−1) 5−1(−1) 3−1(−1) 2−1 = −1. 2. h = (1 2 3) ∈ S12 is even because σ(h) = (−1)3−1 = 1. 3. To find out directly if gh is even or odd we first need to write it as a product of disjoint cycles because our result only holds for products of disjoint cycles. Now, gh = (1 7 3 4 2)(9 5 6)(8 11)(1 2 3) = (2 4)(3 7)(5 6 9)(8 11), so σ(gh) = (−1) 2−1(−1) 2−1(−1) 3−1(−1) 2−1 = −1, so gh is odd. However, we could calculate σ(gh) more easily (when we know σ(g) and σ(h)) by remembering that σ is a homomorphism: σ(gh) = σ(g)σ(h) = (−1)(1) = −1. 4. Every 3-cycle is even. 5. Any product of even permutations is even. Proof of Proposition 7.2.5. The signature of a cycle of length r is just (−1)r−1. For any cycle c of length r we know that c−1 is just c written backwards, so c −1 is also a cycle of length r. Hence σ(c−1) = (−1) r = σ(c). Now any permutation g can be written as a product of disjoint cycles g = c1c2⋯cm, and we have seen that g−1 = c −1 1 c−1 2 ⋯c−1 m . Hence σ(g−1) = σ(c−1 1 )σ(c −1 2 )⋯σ(c −1 m ) = σ(c1)σ(c2)⋯σ(cm) = σ(g).
